Amazon selected the list of 20 finalists from a stack of over 235 applications submitted by Mexican, Canadian and American local officials.

How are you?
I'm good. Everything is good. Do you think that this sets back the Players Association? I don't.

I mean, it's not great. You know, if you're going to— if you're going to have a binary here, I would rather not have my executive director have an inappropriate relationship with his sister-in-law who he hired flouting nepotism standards and other things. But in the grand scheme of things, is this going to have any demonstrable effect on the collective bargaining talks? No, I don't. And that's because I get the sense at this point, and we're going to know a lot more tonight after union player leaders meet, I get the sense that they're just going to go with Bruce Meyer, who was Tony Clark's deputy executive director, who already was the one leading all of the labor negotiations. And he's just going to be put in charge. And, you know, there are good elements of that. There are elements of that that make Major League Baseball terrified because Bruce Meyer has proven himself as being an absolute thorn in their sides. And already this was going to be a contentious negotiation because owners want a salary cap and because the players are vehemently against it. So all things considered, no, it's not going to have that big of an effect.

Jeff, do you believe that Tony Clark was an ineffective leader? Because everything I read is that the first CBA that he negotiated was the first big win for the owners. Did the owners look at him as a lightweight?

I think that first CBA was bad, right? That was back in 2017. And not coincidentally, Bruce Meyer got fired right afterward. And he was a veteran of labor wars with the NBA, the NFL, and the NHL. So He had a lot of experience. I mean, Tony Clark did some things well. Tony Clark also, just in terms of leadership, there's been discord at the union. Don Van Natta and I reported a couple of stories last year. One, there's a federal investigation into the MLBPA right now by the Eastern District of New York, which all of your listeners are familiar with living there, but those of us who don't live in New York are much more familiar with now because they've been at the forefront of so many of the sports cases that we've seen. You know, NBA, Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz. They've really taken sports in their purview, and there is an open and ongoing investigation right now. On top of that, we wrote a story in October about a company called Players Way that the MLBPA started. It was a youth baseball initiative. Youth baseball is extraordinarily screwed up in many ways. I could talk with you for an hour about that. This was the MLBPA's rejoinder to that, and they spent millions of dollars and no one went to the events. So if you're a player, you can argue, "Hey, where's our money going? Why is it going toward these places?" And so as a businessman, I don't know how effective he was. As a union leader, he wasn't Marvin Miller, he wasn't Donald Teer, he wasn't Michael Wiener.

You know, it's also interesting that, you know, I've read in a couple of places, well, the concern with Meyer is, you know, he's not a really effervescent front-facing guy. And then I would say, well, Donald Fehr was not the life of the party either.
That's exactly right. Neither was Don Fehr.
Yeah. You don't need that, right? That's not— that's not even important.

No. And I think I'll say this. I have a column going up on ESPN.com soon, and In it, I argue that the most important thing for whoever the leader of the Major League Baseball Players Association is going forward is that they are going to be open-minded and that they are going to be creative and that they are going to be thoughtful. Because if you're being attacked in Major League Baseball with the notion of a salary cap, which you vehemently reject the idea of, players do not want a salary cap, but they're They're playing that with a majority of the public in favor of a salary cap for baseball. So you have to come with ideas that convince owners that right now is not the right time for a cap, that so much good is going on in baseball that we can't drive this thing off the cliff. And if owners are as locked in on the idea of a cap as they are, then the players need to be the ones who are guiding this sport toward compromise. And that's not something that, you know, players have done typically in the past. But, you know, turning over a new leaf like that, I think the public that is so pro-cap at this point, really what they are is pro-game on the field. And that's the ultimate question. Are we going to have games in early April of 2027? If the answer is no, then I think it is one of the great self-inflicted wounds in recent sports memory.

Because baseball's in a, in a good spot. You know, the last time— this doesn't even count 2025— $12 billion industry. So that's the best it's ever done. But here's a question that I posed last week, and maybe you have the answer. I'm sure that people from both sides call Jeff Passan, they call Ken Rosenthal, they call Buster Olney to get their side out. But my question to you, Jeff, is why? This is not something that will be settled by a vote by the public. What does it matter which way the public goes? Why can't they just do their negotiating without putting a pall on the upcoming 2026 season where every fan's worried about if there's going to be a next season?

Well, I think that the Pistons, more than any team in the league, have come back with a point to prove. I think they look back on that series last year, and Mike, you know, we've talked about this as well. That was a rock fight, okay? And it wasn't— and then the Knicks went in there and beat them and all that stuff, okay? But until Brunson made Thompson look that bad on that shot at the end of Game 6, it was very much of a play. He's one of the brightest, um, baseball players I've dealt with in, in New York City. They're gonna— I hope that this injury doesn't turn out to be a lingering thing and he's back when they say he's going to be back. Because, you know, just as I said, the, the Knicks are going nowhere without Brunson playing at a very high level.

The Mets are going nowhere without Lindor playing at a very high level. All right, in, in finishing up, this was the story yesterday, story today. window: Year after year, Los Salgadones would continue to throw parties like that first one. Americans would return home, talk of the tacos, the town, their teeth. What was once a town of about 750 when Magaña first arrived is now crammed with clinics, hotels, restaurants, and pharmacies. Today, young dentists and souvenir vendors from all over Mexico continue to migrate to town in hopes of finding stable work. And the tourists keep coming in droves.

In winter, it's too much people and they make lines, and that's uncomfortable for them, but they don't care. They make the lines, you know, and they still coming because they find dental services good, a good price and everything, and very handsome doctors. We live from the tourists, you know.

We live from the tourists. It's a sentiment I heard from everyone in town. Teenagers will run to the border after school to sell trinkets to people waiting in line to go home. Women will walk up and down the line selling handmade sweaters and hot meals. And on the American side, the Quechan Tribe manages a casino resort. It's a popular spot for dental tourists who try their hand at the slot machines in between appointments.

I think Agritones is a good town. It's become a better town than it was before. You know, we really don't have a lot of, like, scenic views or, like, anything touristic. But the people are really, like, they're really, like, hardworking people. And they're also, they like to party, you know? They like to have good times also.

Street promoter Alberto moved back to the area 8 years ago, in part to be closer to his family after a road accident in Cancún made it difficult for him to walk. He told me he gets discounted dental care from the clinics that employ him, but he's been putting off amputating his leg for years because of the cost of surgery.
For molars, we vary anywhere from $120 to some of us— some of us are making like $500 or $800 a week.
I asked Alberto what he thought about the town's transformation into Molar City.

I think dental has helped Algodones a lot, but I think people just make their money and they go somewhere else, you know? They go live it up somewhere else. Because a lot of these doctors have become millionaires.

Many of those original dentists live in mansions complete with indoor courtyards and pools. In addition to their dental practice, certain families in town own many of the hotels, restaurants, and pharmacies here. But zoom out of the town center and you'll see mostly unpaved roads and humble homes. There's this 18th-century paleontologist, Georges Cuvier. He has this famous quote about teeth. "Show me your teeth," he said, "and I will tell you who you are." It's true. That from teeth alone, a dental anthropologist can gather all sorts of information. They can decipher migration patterns and cultural norms. They can tell if you ate with your fingers or if you endured famine. Our teeth are biographies. They hold facts about ourselves, facts we may not even recognize while we're alive. I'm curious how you would describe Your relationship to your teeth?
You know, my relationship with my teeth was, you know, I didn't really take the time on a daily basis to have good dental care. I haven't truly smiled in probably 10 years.

Hablaba Pedro Sánchez, muy ocupado, concediendo a los medios internacionales las entrevistas que niega sistemáticamente a los periodistas de aquí, cuando nuestro país fue noticia por otro motivo distinto a los habituales desplantes de nuestro presidente contra Trump.

El rostro de Noelia Castillo con esos enormes ojos anegados de desesperanza se coló en las webs y las redes sociales de medio mundo. España fue noticia porque en este país una joven de 25 años con serios problemas mentales y acreditadas pulsiones suicidas recibió la ayuda de los poderes públicos para lograr su terrible objetivo.

Mientras no le vimos la cara a Noelia, su caso era apenas una línea perdida entre la maraña de informaciones que deglutimos cada día. Un padre y una hija pleiteaban en los tribunales por la eutanasia que solicitaba la joven. La cosa apenas pasaba de disputa familiar, pero en cuanto la muchacha salió a los medios, tomó cuerpo el drama de la eutanasia.

Hay películas, episodios de series de televisión e incluso algunos anuncios comerciales en otros países que se empeñan en presentarnos el rostro amable de la eutanasia, el morir bonito, la supuesta dignidad, la libre elección del momento del adiós. Pero el caso de Noelia ha barrido de golpe tanta propaganda, el dolor que hoy sentimos por ella.

Y el estremecimiento que nos ha causado su muerte es el que ignoramos mientras debatimos sobre la eutanasia como una más de las banderas de la guerra cultural, como los toros, el cambio climático o el consumo de carne de vacuna.

El caso de Noelia no es una excepción, puede haber más en el futuro, porque la ley sobre este asunto tan fundamental se hizo como todo, deprisa, corriendo y sin querer escuchar a quienes están tratando con este drama día a día. Tampoco constituyen una excepción las pulsiones suicidas de esta desgraciada muchacha.

Los problemas de salud mental de nuestros adolescentes se han multiplicado en los últimos años, al igual que la cifra de suicidios. Hoy el suicidio es la principal causa externa de muerte entre jóvenes y adolescentes. Las consultas y las hospitalizaciones psiquiátricas se han disparado a raíz de la pandemia, pero era una tendencia que ya venía de atrás.
Después de la polémica de estos días, me pregunto a cuántos de esos miles de jóvenes con problemas se les ha animado a pensar que su solución puede ser la que Noelia buscó con tanta tenacidad.

Presentar la muerte voluntaria como algo bonito o noble o como un canto al libre albedrío es una atrocidad, siempre y en cualquier circunstancia. Cuando se trata de una joven de 25 años, pero también cuando se trata de un anciano enfermo cuya vida merece la misma dignidad y consideración. No hace falta ser creyente para entender que la vida es el mayor don que recibimos y merece toda la protección que seamos capaces de brindarle.

La respuesta del gobierno a la terrible conmoción que ha causado el suicidio asistido de Noelia ha sido el anuncio de que se van a acelerar los plazos de la eutanasia para los casos urgentes. Curiosa urgencia por parte de un gobierno que demoró más allá de lo razonable las ayudas que los enfermos de ELA tuvieron que reclamar durante años. No sé si pretenden convencernos de que hubiera sido mejor

Menthol activates cold-sensitive nerve receptors in the mouth, throat, and airways, creating a cooling sensation when you inhale smoke.. It's a mild anesthetic numbing effect that reduces pain and irritation from hot, harsh cigarette smoke, making it feel smoother. A dramatic shift hit Nebraska's refugee resettlement system after the January 2025 federal freeze on admissions, turning an active pipeline into a limited operation with real human costs.

Since the freeze, Nebraska's agencies have faced funding losses and program cuts that disrupted services for refugees, forcing shifts in how they operate. Funding collapses pushed agencies to absorb costs, shutter programs, or layoff staff, with organizations like ICR1 and Catholic Social Services of Southern Nebraska feeling the impact while private philanthropy steps in to fill gaps.

Interviews with locals reveal the human toll, refugees facing food insecurity, gaps in health coverage, housing challenges, and barriers to reuniting with family due to limited intake capacity. Federal prioritization of white South African refugees since mid-2025 has added ethical concerns and complicated agency decisions, with some organizations pausing intake as a result.

That policy emphasis created a moral dilemma for local agencies and contributed to pauses or reductions in refugee intake. Refugees in Nebraska confront increased poverty and barriers to essential services, including tighter SNAP and Medicaid eligibility, greater reliance on private funds, and new costs for services like green card applications at CSS.

Historically, Nebraska welcomed refugees at a high per capita rate since 2013, and the shift in policy is producing long-term social and economic effects on both refugees and local service providers. Experts warn that rebuilding Nebraska's refugee infrastructure will take years, as three of four state agencies paused resettlement and funding remains uncertain under future administrations.

By 2026, four Nebraska resettlement agencies had reduced activity or halted resettlement, with advocates fearing a lengthy rebuilding process and uncertain capacity to resume full operations. Tightening federal policy, MIS, disinformation, and administrative barriers have deepened hardship for refugees, affecting food security, health coverage, and housing stability.

The freeze also led to canceled flights for cleared refugees, suspended funding for new arrivals and mass layoffs across resettlement agencies, pushing programs to rely more on private philanthropy and contracts.

Security by obscurity is when you hide how a security measure works, not when you keep some part of it a secret. So I'm going to repeat that multiple times in different ways with some examples. So certain types of security controls like encryption, for example, have two components, the mechanism and the key.

In encryption, the mechanism is the algorithm and the key is, well, the key. So the real question is whether you're hiding the mechanism or you're hiding the key when you obscure something or you make it secret. So it's fine for there to be secrets inside of security systems. when we're talking about security by obscurity, we want to make sure that hiding how the mechanism works isn't the basis for the security. We want the basis for the security to be the key. So that is the central point here. This is the most important concept. And we're going to explore that with some examples here. So if you hide how an encryption algorithm works, you're using security by obscurity.

And that's bad and we all agree on that. But what about these examples? What about frequency hopping on a radio system to avoid eavesdropping? what the algorithm is for making the changes. So is that security by security?
